specAnchors.text: describe the reactions of hydrochloric acid, sulfuric acid and nitric acid with metals, bases and metal carbonates (excluding the reactions between nitric acid and metals) to form salts

primer.text: From Acids, Bases & Salt Preparations you know the solubility rules and the proton picture of acids and bases. This note catalogues the three great acid reaction families: with metals above hydrogen, with bases, and with metal carbonates. Each family has its own products, its own equations, and one unmistakable sign, the fizzing of carbonate reactions.

modules.title: Reactions of acids with metals
modules.opening: Only metals above hydrogen in the reactivity series react with dilute acids, and the more reactive the metal, the more vigorous the reaction. Potassium and sodium react dangerously fast, so they are never used in school glassware. In every such reaction the products are a salt and hydrogen gas, summarised as metal + acid giving salt + hydrogen.
keyPoints: A metal must sit above hydrogen in the series to react with dilute acids.
The more reactive the metal, the more vigorous its reaction with acid.
Potassium and sodium react with acids explosively.
Acid-metal reactions always give a salt and hydrogen.
Sulfuric acid makes sulfate salts and hydrochloric acid makes chloride salts.

low.restatement: The reactivity series is the gate: metals below hydrogen never react with dilute acids, and metals above it react faster the higher they sit. Every successful reaction makes a salt and bubbles of hydrogen.
low.analogy: Think of a queue at a ride with a height bar: below the bar, hydrogen, no entry; above it, the taller the metal, the wilder the ride.
low.examPointer: Expect equation-writing from the summary table: swap the acid to change the salt name, and always add hydrogen as the second product.

medium.restatement: Position above hydrogen is the licence to react, and vigour rises with reactivity, which is why potassium and sodium react explosively and are excluded from classroom acids. The products are systematic: a salt named after the acid, chloride from hydrochloric acid and sulfate from sulfuric acid, plus hydrogen gas, following the general equation metal + acid gives salt + hydrogen.
medium.analogy: Treat the acid as a name-stamp: hydrochloric stamps chlorides and sulfuric stamps sulfates onto whatever metal enters, with hydrogen always released as the by-product.
medium.examPointer: Compare-table questions ask for products at speed, so memorise the acid-to-salt mapping before revising individual equations.

modules.title: Acids with bases and metal carbonates
sourceHeadings: Reactions of Acids with Metal Carbonates
modules.opening: When an acid meets a base, a neutralisation occurs and the products are a salt and water; metal oxides and metal hydroxides both act as bases. With metal carbonates there is a third product: the fizzing of carbon dioxide gas, which makes carbonate reactions unmistakable. In each family the salt name tracks the acid, giving chlorides, sulfates or nitrates.
keyPoints: Acid + base gives salt + water, and the reaction is a neutralisation.
Both metal oxides and metal hydroxides can play the base role.
Hydrochloric acid gives chlorides, sulfuric acid sulfates and nitric acid nitrates.
Acid + metal carbonate gives salt + carbon dioxide + water.
Effervescence of carbon dioxide marks the carbonate reaction.

low.restatement: Bases mop up acids into salt and water, and carbonates add the fizz of carbon dioxide on top of that pair. Either way the salt's name comes from the acid involved: hydrochloric gives chlorides, sulfuric gives sulfates, and nitric gives nitrates, so naming the salt never requires guessing.
low.analogy: The carbonate reaction is the only one that throws a party, with visible bubbles; the base reaction is the quiet one that just leaves salt and water behind when the guests go home.
low.examPointer: Spot-the-family questions hinge on the products: water present means a base was used, bubbles mean a carbonate, and hydrogen means a metal.

medium.restatement: The base route is neutralisation: metal oxides and hydroxides accept the acid's protons to give a salt and water, with the salt named by the acid, chloride, sulfate or nitrate. The carbonate route adds carbon dioxide, whose effervescence distinguishes it immediately, following the general pattern acid + metal carbonate gives salt + carbon dioxide + water, with nitric acid excluded from the metal family only.
medium.analogy: Picture two recipes sharing the same base ingredients, salt and water, where the carbonate version simply adds a fizzing extra course of carbon dioxide.
medium.examPointer: The exam hint is the giveaway: any acid reaction producing effervescence must involve a metal carbonate making carbon dioxide.

glossary.definition: The ionic compound made when an acid's hydrogen is replaced by a metal or ammonium partner.
A substance such as a metal oxide or hydroxide that neutralises an acid to salt and water.
The acid-base reaction whose products are a salt and water.
A compound whose acid reaction gives a salt, carbon dioxide and water.
The fizzing caused by a gas escaping from a reaction mixture.
A metal combined with oxygen, which acts as a base in acid reactions.
The salt family produced when hydrochloric acid reacts.
The salt family produced when nitric acid reacts.
